subject: Neurology
vignette: A 35-year-old man has had a painless draining right ear for months. Otoscopy shows a whitish mass in the middle ear and a perforation of the tympanic membrane. Audiometry demonstrates a conductive hearing loss on the right.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: An invasive infection of the mastoid with osteomyelitis
Endolymphatic hydrops causing episodic vertigo and tinnitus
A vestibular schwannoma arising from the eighth cranial nerve
An acute bacterial infection with a bulging erythematous tympanic membrane
Keratinized squamous epithelium in the middle ear that can erode the ossicles

explanation_correct: A cholesteatoma is an abnormal growth of keratinized squamous epithelium in the middle ear, described as skin in the wrong place. It classically presents with painless otorrhea and can erode the ossicles, producing conductive hearing loss. It is usually acquired, from a retraction pocket or a perforation that allows epithelial migration.

explanation_incorrect.A: Invasive infection with osteomyelitis describes malignant necrotizing otitis externa in diabetics, not a painless keratinizing middle ear mass.
explanation_incorrect.B: Endolymphatic hydrops is Ménière disease, which causes vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus rather than a middle ear mass with conductive loss.
explanation_incorrect.C: A vestibular schwannoma is an eighth nerve tumor causing sensorineural loss and vertigo, not a keratin-filled middle ear lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Acute bacterial otitis media produces fever, pain, and a bulging erythematous membrane, not a chronic painless mass with a perforation.

educationalObjective: Cholesteatoma is keratinized squamous epithelium in the middle ear that causes painless otorrhea and conductive loss through ossicular erosion.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient with long-standing eustachian tube dysfunction develops a tympanic membrane retraction pocket. Over time, keratinizing squamous epithelium accumulates in the middle ear with gradual ossicular erosion and conductive hearing loss. There is no history of tympanic membrane perforation or otitis media.
question: Which of the following best classifies this cholesteatoma?

options.text: Secondary acquired cholesteatoma due to tympanic membrane perforation
Primary acquired cholesteatoma due to a retraction pocket from eustachian tube dysfunction
Congenital cholesteatoma present from birth
Iatrogenic cholesteatoma after tympanostomy tube placement
Malignant cholesteatoma with invasive osteomyelitis

explanation_correct: Primary acquired cholesteatoma results from tympanic membrane retraction pockets that form because of eustachian tube dysfunction. The retraction pocket traps keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear, where it erodes ossicles and causes conductive loss. This differs from secondary acquired cholesteatoma, which follows a tympanic membrane perforation that permits epithelial migration.

explanation_incorrect.A: Secondary acquired cholesteatoma arises from a tympanic membrane perforation allowing squamous epithelial migration; this patient has a retraction pocket without perforation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Congenital cholesteatoma is present from birth and is not due to a retraction pocket caused by eustachian tube dysfunction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Iatrogenic cholesteatoma from tympanostomy tubes is not the described mechanism; retraction from eustachian tube dysfunction defines the primary acquired form.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cholesteatoma is not classified as malignant with osteomyelitis; that description fits malignant otitis externa instead.

educationalObjective: Primary acquired cholesteatoma arises from a retraction pocket due to eustachian tube dysfunction, while secondary acquired follows a perforation.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 55-year-old woman has brief episodes of spinning vertigo that last less than a minute and are triggered by rolling over in bed or looking up. She has no hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurologic deficits between episodes.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ménière disease
Vestibular neuritis
Central vertigo due to a brainstem stroke
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
Acute otitis media

explanation_correct: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by semicircular canal debris and produces episodic vertigo lasting one minute or less that is provoked by certain head movements. It is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike maneuver and treated with the Epley maneuver. The absence of hearing loss, tinnitus, and neurologic findings supports a peripheral positional cause.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ménière disease causes longer episodes of vertigo with sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, the triad remembered as men wear vests, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.B: Vestibular neuritis produces continuous vertigo lasting days rather than brief, position-triggered episodes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Central vertigo from a stroke causes nystagmus of any direction not suppressible with fixation and neurologic findings such as diplopia or ataxia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acute otitis media is a middle ear infection with fever and a bulging tympanic membrane, not positional vertigo.

educationalObjective: BPPV causes brief positional vertigo from canal debris and is diagnosed with Dix-Hallpike and treated with Epley.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 50-year-old man has recurrent episodes of severe spinning vertigo lasting about 30 minutes, accompanied by ringing in the right ear and a feeling of fullness. Over time he has developed right-sided sensorineural hearing loss.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Ménière disease due to endolymphatic hydrops
BPPV due to displaced canal debris
Vestibular neuritis due to viral inflammation
Cholesteatoma with ossicular erosion
Presbycusis due to age-related hair cell loss

explanation_correct: Ménière disease results from endolymphatic hydrops, an increase in endolymph in the inner ear. It produces a classic triad of episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus, often with a sensation of ear fullness, remembered as men wear vests. The combination of vertigo with auditory symptoms fits this diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: BPPV causes brief positional vertigo lasting a minute or less and does not cause hearing loss or tinnitus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Vestibular neuritis causes acute prolonged vertigo without the auditory features of tinnitus and hearing loss.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cholesteatoma causes conductive rather than sensorineural loss with painless otorrhea and a middle ear mass.
explanation_incorrect.E: Presbycusis produces gradual bilateral symmetric sensorineural loss in the elderly without vertigo or tinnitus.

educationalObjective: Ménière disease is endolymphatic hydrops causing the triad of vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A patient presents with vertigo. Examination shows unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus that diminishes when the patient fixes gaze on a stationary target. There are no other neurologic findings such as diplopia, ataxia, or dysmetria.
question: Which of the following best localizes the lesion?

options.text: Central vertigo from a brainstem stroke, with nystagmus suppressible by fixation
Central vertigo from demyelination, with unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus
Peripheral vertigo from inner ear pathology, with horizontal-torsional, unidirectional, suppressible nystagmus
Central vertigo from a posterior fossa tumor, with no neurologic findings
Peripheral vertigo from Ménière disease, with purely vertical nystagmus

explanation_correct: Peripheral vertigo arises from inner ear pathology such as vestibular neuritis, BPPV, or Ménière disease. Its nystagmus is mixed horizontal-torsional, never purely torsional or vertical, does not change direction, and is suppressible with visual fixation. The absence of neurologic findings further supports a peripheral rather than central lesion.

explanation_incorrect.A: Central nystagmus is not suppressible with visual fixation, and a brainstem stroke would typically produce additional neurologic findings.
explanation_incorrect.B: Central lesions produce nystagmus of any direction that is not suppressible, not the unidirectional horizontal-torsional and suppressible pattern described.
explanation_incorrect.D: A posterior fossa tumor is a central cause and would generally produce non-suppressible nystagmus and neurologic findings such as ataxia or dysmetria.
explanation_incorrect.E: Peripheral nystagmus is never purely vertical; it is mixed horizontal-torsional, and Ménière disease would also include hearing loss and tinnitus.

educationalObjective: Peripheral vertigo produces unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressible with fixation and no neurologic findings.
